title: The Phasing Call
primary_metric: hours of autonomous-flight/consumables reserve remaining at docking per calendar day of launch-window phase-angle flexibility gained

options.A: The Fast-Track — a direct, few-orbit rendezvous profile that reaches the station fastest and preserves the most autonomous-flight/consumables reserve, at the cost of a narrow launch-window phase-angle tolerance
options.B: The Phasing Climb — a multi-orbit parking-orbit phasing rendezvous profile that tolerates the widest range of launch-day phase angles, at the cost of spending far more of the vehicle's fixed reserve reaching the station

_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC §4
protagonist: Talia Brooks, Trajectory Analyst, Meridian Launch Systems

replaces.reason: the-transfer-window's balance test failed by ~800x (margin_pct=15940.5), a fixed, structural chemical-vs-electric-propulsion transit-time asymmetry that cannot be retuned without fabricating a number (see cases/the-transfer-window/RESEARCH_LOG.md, 'RETUNE PASS — 2026-08-31'). the-transfer-window is left unmodified as the historical record. This case keeps the same protagonist/career/company/skill group and swaps the deciding asymmetry to a same-propulsion-system rendezvous-timing-strategy comparison, which real precedent shows differs by a realistic few-x, not several-hundred-x.

deliverables.text: A conversion of the client station's tracked position (Appendix A) from the polar coordinate its tracking radar reports -- a bearing and range from the tracking site -- into a rectangular coordinate, with your conversion work shown in full.

A pair of parametric position equations, x(t) and y(t), for each rendezvous profile (the Fast-Track and the Phasing Climb), using each profile's stated angular catch-up rate from Appendix B, with the parameter identified by name and explained in plain terms (what it represents physically, and what values it ranges over for each profile's full rendezvous).

For each profile, the rectangular (Cartesian) equation of the vehicle's closing path, found by eliminating the parameter from that profile's D2 equations, showing every algebraic step -- followed by a solved check, using that rectangular equation, of the elapsed time at which each profile actually reaches the station's D1 rectangular position, with your algebra shown in full.

An autonomous-flight/consumables-reserve calculation for each profile: what percent of Appendix C's fixed total allowance is used up by the time each profile reaches docking (using your D3 elapsed-transit-time figures), and what percent remains as reserve.

A graphed polar boundary for each profile's phase-angle tolerance band (Appendix D): using the 0-360 degree phase-angle circle centered on the moment of liftoff, graph each profile's workable phase-angle band as a polar equation, stating that equation explicitly, so the two bands' relative widths are visible on a single polar plot.

A launch-window calendar calculation for each profile: using your D5 graphed phase-angle bands and the station's orbital period from Appendix D, how many days in a 30-day launch calendar fall inside each profile's workable phase-angle window, with your arithmetic shown.

A single primary-metric comparison table -- hours of reserve margin remaining at docking (from D4) per calendar day of launch-window flexibility (from D6) -- built for both profiles, with the division shown for each.
A recommendation to Meridian's launch director, defended using your D7 result, stating plainly what would have to change about either profile for your recommendation to flip.

balance.argument_a: The Fast-Track reaches the station in a small number of orbits, leaving the largest possible share of the vehicle's fixed autonomous-flight/consumables allowance untouched at docking (Appendix C). Real operational precedent (the modern 4-orbit/~6-hour and 2-orbit/~3-hour Soyuz profiles) shows this is the profile actually flown whenever launch conditions allow, precisely because it preserves the largest contingency reserve for a failed first approach or a docking hold-off -- a real, quantifiable safety and schedule-resilience margin.
balance.argument_b: The Phasing Climb tolerates a 270-degree band of initial phase angle versus the Fast-Track's 30-degree band (Appendix D) -- roughly 22.5 of every 30 calendar days are workable launch attempts for the Phasing Climb against roughly 2.5 for the Fast-Track. Real orbital-mechanics precedent documents phasing-orbit rendezvous durations spanning roughly 1 to 5 days depending on how far off the phase angle starts at liftoff, because the vehicle can simply fly more or fewer phasing orbits to absorb the mismatch. A launch provider that can launch on 9 times as many of its scheduled days avoids the real, recurring cost of a scrubbed or slipped attempt (weather holds, range conflicts, technical delays).
balance.margin_basis: Primary metric: hours of autonomous-flight/consumables reserve remaining at docking (D4), divided by the number of days per 30-day launch calendar that fall inside that profile's workable phase-angle tolerance band (D6) -- a ratio of two independently-sourced quantities, not a single total. reserve_hours_remaining(profile) = total_allowance_hours - modeled_transit_hours(profile); workable_days_per_30(profile) = 30 * (phase_angle_tolerance_degrees(profile) / 360); metric(profile) = reserve_hours_remaining(profile) / workable_days_per_30(profile). Compare metric(A) vs metric(B) as a percent difference.
balance.margin_note: COMPUTED 2026-08-31 (case-research stage). Inputs, all real and cited (see RESEARCH_LOG.md): total_allowance_hours = 4.2 days * 24 = 100.8 h [S10, primary Soyuz Crew Operations Manual]. modeled_transit_hours(A, Fast-Track) = 6 h [S2, operational 4-orbit/6-hour Soyuz profile]. modeled_transit_hours(B, Phasing Climb) = 60 h / 2.5 days [S5, Cygnus NG-19's real Aug-2023 rendezvous]. phase_angle_tolerance(A) = 30 deg, phase_angle_tolerance(B) = 270 deg [S11, NASASpaceFlight.com 2012 reporting on Progress M-16M's fast-rendezvous test -- the most authoritative numeric tolerance-band figure found after a genuine multi-query search, graded MEDIUM since the underlying Russian source document is described but not named]. reserve_hours(A) = 100.8-6 = 94.8 h (94.05%); reserve_hours(B) = 100.8-60 = 40.8 h (40.48%). workable_days_per_30(A) = 30*(30/360) = 2.5; workable_days_per_30(B) = 30*(270/360) = 22.5. metric(A) = 94.8/2.5 = 37.92 h/day; metric(B) = 40.8/22.5 = 1.81 h/day. percent difference = (37.92-1.81)/1.81*100 = 1991.18%. WINNER under this metric: Option A, The Fast-Track. THIS FAILS SPEC SECTION 2's ~20% BALANCE CAP by roughly two orders of magnitude (though less severely than the-transfer-window's ~15,940% failure). DIAGNOSIS: the concept sheet's pre-research expectation ('both terms differ by only a few-x') held for the reserve-hours term (real values differ by only ~2.3x, both landing in the 40-94% range, because Soyuz's real 4.2-day total autonomy budget is generous relative to either profile's real hours-to-days transit time) but did NOT hold for the phase-angle-tolerance term, where the real, sourced figures (30 deg vs 270 deg) differ by 9x. Because the primary metric is a straight ratio (reserve divided by workable-days), a 9x denominator asymmetry is not offset by a 2.3x numerator asymmetry -- they compound rather than partially cancel, producing the ~20x blowout. Tested the full plausible range of real-precedent transit-time choices found during research (3-6 h for Fast-Track; 24-60 h for Phasing Climb): every combination lands the ratio between roughly 11x and 21x -- the blowout is structural to combining a real ~9x phase-angle-tolerance ratio with a real total-autonomy budget too large relative to both profiles' real transit times to ever produce a compensating reserve-hours asymmetry near 9x, not an artifact of which specific real figure was chosen within its documented range. No number here was tuned away from its real, cited value to chase a target margin -- this is a genuine finding for case-qa/case-readiness to weigh, most likely requiring the same kind of redesign or retune review that the-transfer-window itself received.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: No public contract exists for the fictional Meridian Launch Systems; the 96-hour deadline (MA2) is a documented good-faith estimate anchored directly to Soyuz's real, cited 100.8-hour (4.2-day) total autonomous-flight allowance [S10], set a few hours inside that real hardware ceiling. Tier 2 probe 5 reports this dial as breaking the 20% cap under both +/-50% flex, but that is a restatement of the case's own MCS-46-waived baseline margin (~1991% before any flex, per case.json.balance_test_waiver) -- the dial itself does not meaningfully move the margin's order of magnitude. The one real effect: flexing -50% to 48 hours disqualifies the Phasing Climb outright on the deadline floor, which case.md Appendix E's own MA2 sensitivity note already discloses in prose ('a deadline tightened below ~60 hours would begin to threaten the Phasing Climb's flyability').

No public contract term of this kind is published for a real commercial LEO resupply mission; the 15% reserve floor (MA3) is a documented good-faith estimate in line with typical aerospace mission-assurance contingency conventions. Tier 2 probe 5 reports this dial as breaking the 20% cap under both +/-50% flex, but this is the same MCS-46-waived baseline margin recurring, not a new instability caused by MA3 -- neither profile's feasibility flips at 0.075 or 0.225. Per case.md Appendix E's own MA3 sensitivity note, this floor would have to rise above roughly 40% (well above any published contingency convention found during research) before it could disqualify the Phasing Climb outright.

derived.twist_additive_score_note: sensitivity_model.py's evaluate_twist() illustrates the FACILITATOR.md Twist: if D7's ratio (reserve-hours divided by workable-launch-days) were instead built as an evenly-weighted (50/50) additive score of the same two real quantities (reserve-fraction of total allowance, and phase-angle-tolerance-fraction of the full 360-degree range), Option A scores approximately 0.512 and Option B scores approximately 0.577 -- the Phasing Climb wins under that alternate, equally-legitimate metric construction, even though nothing about the real-world figures changed. This is a facilitator-only illustration of why the metric's shape (ratio vs. sum) drives the result, not a claim that case.md's own D7 ratio metric is wrong.
derived.twist_additive_score_fragility_note: TIER 2 PROBE 4 FINDING (2026-08-31, adversarial subagent review): the 0.512-vs-0.577 flip is a knife-edge result, not a robust one -- only about 12.7% apart (vs. D7's ~20x/1991% landslide), and dependent on the exact 50/50 weighting. Solving for the weight w on the reserve-fraction term at which the two additive scores tie gives w = approximately 0.554; a mildly different, equally defensible weighting (w = 0.60, i.e. weighting reserve somewhat more heavily than launch-day count, since reserve is a safety margin) flips the winner back to the Fast-Track. This is unlike D7's own ratio result, which case.json.balance.margin_note documents as stable across the entire plausible range of real transit-time figures (~11x to ~21x, never flipping). FACILITATOR.md's Twist section now discloses this fragility explicitly so a facilitator does not present the additive-score flip as equally robust to D7's real result.

balance_test_waiver.reason: Per MCS-46: the margin (1991.18%) is real, honestly researched, and structurally driven (a real ~9x phase-angle-tolerance ratio compounding with a real reserve-hours ratio inside a straight-division metric), not a modeling shortcut. Waived because (1) the setup still forces genuine multi-step work -- sourcing and combining two independently-derived real quantities (a fixed autonomy budget minus modeled transit time; a phase-angle tolerance converted to workable launch-calendar days) into one ratio, cross-checked against primary orbital-mechanics/mission-ops documents, is not a plug-and-chug exercise -- and (2) the size of the gap (~20x) is not guessable from the premise alone: a student's naive intuition (fast vs. slow rendezvous should trade off reserve time against schedule flexibility by a similar, comparable amount) is actively wrong until the real 9x tolerance-band asymmetry is computed, which is itself the pedagogical payoff. Per project owner: 'a case that is one obvious answer is not ideal... but in this case for this topic, we can give a little' -- explicitly scoped to this case, not a general relaxation, and explicitly not retroactive to other cases with a similarly lopsided margin.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Client station's tracked bearing and range at the moment of the decision
modeling_assumptions.basis: No real, named LEO client station of this kind exists under contract with a company like Meridian; a stated scenario tracking readout, chosen to give a non-trivial D1 polar-to-rectangular conversion.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Changes the D1 rectangular coordinate and the specific D3 elapsed-time answer for both profiles equally; does not change which profile wins the D6/D7 ratio, since both profiles close on the same tracked position and the ratio is driven by Appendix B/C/D's real figures, not this one.

modeling_assumptions.basis: No public contract exists for the fictional Meridian Launch Systems; anchored directly to Soyuz's real published 4.2-day (100.8-hour) total autonomous-flight allowance (S10), set a few hours inside that real hardware ceiling the way a real mission-assurance contract would build in slack.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Both profiles' modeled transit times (6 h and 60 h) sit well inside 96 h, so neither option is disqualified by the deadline alone; only a deadline tightened below ~60 hours would begin to threaten the Phasing Climb's flyability.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Minimum required autonomous-flight/consumables reserve remaining at docking
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public contract term of this kind is published for a real commercial LEO resupply mission; a stated contingency fraction in line with typical aerospace mission-assurance conventions, disclosed as an assumption rather than a sourced figure.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Both profiles clear this floor by a wide margin under this case's real, sourced transit-time figures (Fast-Track ~94% reserve, Phasing Climb ~40% reserve); this assumption would have to rise above ~40% before it could disqualify the Phasing Climb outright.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Each rendezvous profile is modeled as a single constant angular catch-up rate over its full transit, rather than as its real multi-burn sequence
modeling_assumptions.value_used: Constant rate, ~0.187 deg/min (~11.2 deg/hour), derived from the two real orbital periods (S9, S10)
modeling_assumptions.basis: Both real profiles this case is modeled on fly a short sequence of discrete burns, not one continuous rate. Modeling each as a single constant-rate parametric arc is a stated simplification appropriate to this case's Pre-Calculus/Polar-and-Parametric skill target; the underlying wait-time/lead-angle relationship it draws on is real, published orbital-mechanics math (S6).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Does not affect the D4/D5/D6 reserve-and-flexibility comparison, which is driven by each profile's real, sourced total transit time (Appendix B), not by how that transit time is broken into individual burns. Only affects the D2/D3 algebra, which models one arc instead of several.
